sender_context: New Yorker staff writer who had never met Gates
what_it_did: Skipped Microsoft PR and wrote straight to Gates's widely known address. Introduced himself as the writer working on the New Yorker piece about him and opened with a question about what makes email unique as a medium, a topic Gates loved.
the_ask: Answer one open question about email
outcome: A weeks-long email correspondence (three or four exchanges a week) that became the New Yorker article 'E-mail from Bill' (January 1994).

sender_context: Special projects editor at Inc., unknown to Cuban
subject_line: For Inc. mag: Can you pls. Share 3 Tips to Manage Your Inbox?
what_it_did: Drafted ten versions with a colleague, then sent the entire request as the subject line. The body held only his signature so Cuban could see who was asking.
response: Reply in 7 minutes (sent 4:03 pm, answered 4:10 pm)
outcome: Cuban's tips ran in Inc. Hagerman distilled the lesson to: be clear, be brief, be direct.

sender_context: 25-year-old first-time founder of Factmata, no US network
what_it_did: Opened by apologizing for the cold message, then stacked credibility fast: Google-backed, three NLP researchers with 30+ published papers. Tied the pitch to Cuban's own recent public comments on fake news. Under 150 words.
the_ask: Permission to share more about the company
outcome: $250K immediately and another $250K nine months later. Ghulati raised his whole ~$1M seed through cold email; he also emailed Craig Newmark and Biz Stone.
tactics: humility; credibility-first; researched-personalization; tiny-ask; short; timing

sender_context: CEO of Mapistry (environmental-compliance SaaS)
what_it_did: Her first email two years earlier was vague and went nowhere. The rewrite used a plain descriptive subject, led with the problem (compliance run on spreadsheets, multi-million-dollar lawsuit risk), then named Fortune 500 customers, a $3.7B market and specific growth numbers.
the_ask: A 30-minute call, with two specific times offered
response: Lemkin replied and later published it as one of the two best cold emails he had received
outcome: Lemkin funded the company; Mapistry raised a $2.5M seed. The same template, tweaked per investor, hit a reported 33% success rate.

sender_context: Contact-center startup at roughly $1M ARR
what_it_did: Under 200 words. Led with the ARR figure, named real customer case studies, sketched the go-to-market and gave strong but unhyped growth metrics.
outcome: Lemkin became Talkdesk's first venture investor; the company later reached a ~$10B valuation.

sender_context: Founder of Mangomint (salon and spa software), early stage
what_it_did: Cold-emailed with early customer revenue as the hook.
outcome: A small early investment; Lemkin stayed involved and Mangomint later raised a $35M Series B.

sender_context: Founder of the 20VC podcast and fund
what_it_did: Sent 53 emails, roughly weekly for a year. Each one varied the personal hook (a whiskey they both liked, a favorite holiday spot, recent results) and he A/B tested which personalization landed. Clear ask, short copy, credibility via audience numbers and past guests.
outcome: Benioff appeared on 20VC in 2023 and publicly credited Stebbings's persistence.

sender_context: Salesperson at a North Carolina systems integrator
what_it_did: Read about salesforce.com in the Wall Street Journal, found Benioff's address and asked whether he could resell the product.
response: Quick reply: no reseller program, but fly to San Francisco and meet
outcome: Hired on the spot as employee #36; stayed a decade and became Salesforce's top global account executive.

recipient_role: Entrepreneur; then owner of the Dallas Mavericks
sender_context: 20-year-old USC student building Box from his dorm room
what_it_did: Emailed essentially every investor he could find. Same pitch to all: storage getting cheaper, internet getting faster, people working across devices. Cuban's streaming-media past made him primed for it.
response: Reply within a few hours, first proposing a data-hosting project together
outcome: Cuban invested $350K before meeting the founders. Box later went public.

sender_context: Founders of Relativity Space (3D-printed rockets)
what_it_did: Pitched an ambitious space company entirely by email.
response: Cuban engaged by email and never met them in person
outcome: $500K initially and a few million in total; Cuban later described the company as worth about $4B.

sender_context: Radiologist who had founded Osh's Affordable Pharmaceuticals
what_it_did: Labeled it honestly in the subject line and pitched a mission Cuban already cared about: generic drugs priced out of reach by middlemen.
outcome: Months of weekly email exchanges; Cuban pushed him to think bigger. It became the Mark Cuban Cost Plus Drug Company (founded 2020, pharmacy launched January 2022).

sender_context: 21-year-old FiscalNote co-founder living in a Motel 6 in Sunnyvale
what_it_did: Sent on a whim after watching Shark Tank. Short and direct: who he was, what FiscalNote did (AI to predict legislative outcomes), how far they'd come.
response: Reply in 45 minutes, followed by detailed questions
outcome: Cuban led the round with $740K; the round grew to about $1.3M.

sender_context: Founder of Clipbook (AI PR monitoring), bootstrapped to $1M ARR
what_it_did: Picked the five best media investors in the world and sent each a one-page pitch: what it does, why legacy tools fall short, what's different, $1M ARR bootstrapped.
response: Only Cuban replied, with about 20 skeptical questions
outcome: Answered every question, then ran a live product demo on Cuban's own company. Raised a $3M seed co-led by Cuban.

sender_context: Co-founder of Mention Mobile (social games), bootstrapping
what_it_did: Found a 2010 Cuban blog post saying he wanted to hear from social-game developers, then sent a short intro: Emmy-winning co-founder, one game shipped, more coming.
the_ask: Introduction and a chance to pitch
response: Reply in about 8 minutes, asking for a concept portfolio and revenue projections
outcome: $250K investment after a couple of months of diligence, plus ongoing advice.

sender_context: CEO of ZergNet
what_it_did: Sent a detailed pitch in the middle of the night.
response: Cuban liked the idea and the detail of the answers
outcome: $30K initially, with more later.

sender_context: CEO of Cultivate (tools for US small businesses)
what_it_did: Cold outreach pitching a startup that helps American small businesses.
outcome: Investment within 72 hours.

recipient_role: Uber co-founder; then starting the 10100 fund
sender_context: YC founder, ex-Uber self-driving ML engineer
what_it_did: Timed it to Kalanick leaving Uber and starting a fund. Framed a trade: Andy gets an angel and mentor; Kalanick backs a former Uber engineer with a unique market insight.
outcome: Andy says more than half of the billionaires and notable people he emails respond.

sender_context: ML engineer
what_it_did: Wrote just as she was starting Insitro and positioned himself as an early employee who would do whatever it took to help the new company succeed.
outcome: Conversation opened (details in source).

sender_context: Founder
what_it_did: Used the same four principles: establish competency, make the ask, be transparent about self-interest, show extra effort.
outcome: Listed by the author among billionaires who responded.

sender_context: Founder
what_it_did: Pitched co-building a startup incubator and, before sending, wrote and published a full blog post arguing why Not Boring should incubate companies.
outcome: The idea wasn't a fit, but the effort earned a real conversation.

sender_context: Then a student; later Managing Director at General Catalyst
what_it_did: Went to Musk directly rather than Tesla staff. Opened with nostalgia (university and graduation) to read as human, not spam; offered sincere, specific appreciation rather than flattery.
the_ask: Interview Musk for a research paper on Tesla's corporate strategy
outcome: Featured in the Cold Email Hall of Fame as a model of a simple, specific ask.

sender_context: Then a student
what_it_did: Cold-emailed asking for an internship.
outcome: Email shown to newsletter subscribers only.

sender_context: Then a student
what_it_did: Cold-emailed Ballmer directly.
outcome: Email shown to newsletter subscribers only.

sender_context: Canadian founder, rejected from the program he was emailing about
what_it_did: After being the first rejected from the Ship It program, he spotted a My First Million casting call for a 'field trip correspondent' and knew Shaan Puri was close to a Founders, Inc. partner. Used that as a reason to offer to film content at the lab; rewrote the email many times.
the_ask: Access to the lab to shoot content
response: Reply the next day granting a one-week pass
outcome: The video he shot impressed them enough to admit him into the same four-week program that had rejected him. He later started the Cold Email Hall of Fame newsletter.

sender_context: University student building a startup
what_it_did: Researched Gauvreau before a university guest talk (including his friendship with Andrew Wilkinson), asked prepared questions in person, then sent a follow-up email to stand out.
outcome: Became a mentor who helped when Haldar moved to SF. Haldar's rule: never ask someone to be your mentor; ask for advice, act on it, report back, repeat.

sender_context: Featured in the Hall of Fame newsletter
what_it_did: Read as authentic and human (passing the two-second spam test), opened a curiosity gap, and referenced Chamath's own early story of walking Sand Hill Road and writing a letter to a VC.
the_ask: Not 'general advice'; a specific request (see source)
outcome: Used by the newsletter to teach authenticity, curiosity gap and deep research.

sender_context: Student rejected for a startup summer internship
what_it_did: Replied to the rejection email instead of moving on. Made a no-downside offer and showed (rather than claimed) willingness: same time commitment, double the effort, available in the office until September.
the_ask: Reconsider, at no risk to them
outcome: Landed the summer internship.

recipient_role: Managing Director, Peak XV Partners (formerly Sequoia Capital India)
sender_context: Startup founder
what_it_did: Bumped into Anandan at a Starbucks, pitched his startup on the spot, then followed up with a sharp cold email.
outcome: Full email shown to subscribers.

sender_context: Featured in the Hall of Fame newsletter
what_it_did: A cold email that opened a string of conversations.
outcome: Cuban became the founder's mentor.

recipient_role: Founder of The Hustle; co-host of My First Million
sender_context: Featured in the Hall of Fame newsletter
what_it_did: Replied to one of Parr's tweets, then followed with a cold DM.
outcome: Shows the same principles work in DMs.

sender: Podcaster from the Hall of Fame community
sender_context: Worked 1:1 with the newsletter author
what_it_did: Cold-emailed a podcast invitation.
outcome: Landed Cowen as a guest.

sender_context: Writer and podcaster; an earlier attempt years before had failed
what_it_did: Made sure Kagan had recently seen his name a couple of times first, then sent a very short interview request; later built rapport over shared interests in replies.
the_ask: An interview for a guest post
outcome: Interview, a podcast appearance, feedback on his blog, a guest post on Kagan's site, and a thank-you box of cookies from Kagan.

sender_context: Founder of upTalkk; ran 'Kabir Cold Emails Millionaires'
what_it_did: Compelling subject line, a timely welcome to India during Bloom's visit, and a brief line of credibility.
outcome: Conversation opened.

sender_context: Founder of upTalkk
what_it_did: A sentence-by-sentence engineered email (breakdown published, archive now offline).
outcome: Conversation opened.

sender_context: Indian conference speaker with a 72-hour window
what_it_did: Visa processing normally took 20+ days; wrote directly to the ambassador asking for a visa within 48 hours.
outcome: Visa stamped in under 36 hours. The author also reports replies from Mark Zuckerberg, Sheryl Sandberg, Vinod Khosla, Jeff Bezos and Justin Trudeau over 500+ cold emails.

sender_context: Middle-schooler building a frequency counter
what_it_did: Found Hewlett in the phone book and called. Introduced himself plainly as a 12-year-old building a frequency counter and asked if there were spare parts.
response: Hewlett laughed, talked about the project and personally arranged the parts
outcome: Parts plus a summer job on HP's assembly line. Jobs later said he never found anyone who refused to help when asked.

sender_context: Schoolgirl in Hereford, UK
channel: handwritten letter (+ email from her father)
what_it_did: An honest handwritten job application listing her love of computers and robots (and backup plans as an Olympic swimmer or chocolate-factory worker). Her father also emailed Google so the letter would reach the right desk.
response: Personal signed reply within about four days
outcome: Pichai encouraged her to keep learning and said he looked forward to her application after school. The exchange went viral.

recipient: CEO of a Silicon Valley startup (reportedly TrueSAN)
sender_context: Recent Princeton graduate in New York
what_it_did: Emailed the CEO repeatedly but never rudely or too often. Upgraded his signature to a legitimate title (event producer with a startup association) and finally said he'd be 'in the neighborhood' and could stop by.
response: CEO agreed to a Tuesday meeting
outcome: Flew standby to California and walked out with a sales job.

recipient: CEOs and public figures (Disney, Comcast, Google, HP CEOs; a former president; Kleiner Perkins's Randy Komisar)
sender_context: Seniors in 'High-Tech Entrepreneurship', challenged to contact the unreachable
what_it_did: Ferriss offered a round-trip ticket anywhere to whoever got answers from the hardest-to-reach person. One student built real rapport with Komisar over several genuine exchanges.
the_ask: Answer a question they'd always wanted to ask
response: Multiple replies, including from people considered unreachable
outcome: Komisar later emailed the student unprompted with a relevant article. Ferriss's point: getting those replies rewires your sense of what's possible.

sender_context: Co-founder and CEO of WayUp
what_it_did: Dug deep enough to find the recipient's obscure water-aerobics past and used it as an absurd, impossible-to-ignore subject line; the body was sharp and credible.
outcome: Part of a pattern of research-heavy outreach; WayUp raised $27.5M+.

sender_context: Founder of the agency Experiment 27
what_it_did: Personalized in multiple places (including company name in the subject), asked prospects about their own successful strategies, hinted at the pain point and positioned himself as a resource rather than hard-selling.
outcome: Helped grow the agency to about $400K in annual revenue within 30 days.

recipient: A brand he'd identified as a perfect-fit client
sender_context: Content-marketing consultant
what_it_did: Casual tone by design; opened by talking about the recipient rather than his offer, showing he'd done his homework.
outcome: A $10,000-per-month retainer.

sender_context: Copywriter
what_it_did: Called herself a 'customer story writer' (a benefit, not a job title), gave a usable customer-story strategy for free inside the email, then listed tech-writing credentials.
outcome: Part of the outreach that grew her business 1,400% in four months.
